nodeData.note: Edexcel International GCSE Biology, Paper 1, code 4 B I 1 slash 1 B. Two hours, 110 marks, 61 percent of the grade. You may use a calculator. There is no formula sheet. Paper 1 covers all five topics, but not the extra content shown in bold with a letter B in the spec. Each branch is one type of question: read the question, find the key words, plan, write, check. Then five spoken questions. Draft: needs review by a biology teacher. (Source: spec pages 7 and 27.)

children.note: State, give and name all mean the same thing: recall a fact. State what is meant by means give a definition. Multiple choice questions start with what, why or which. These test knowledge, which is assessment objective 1. Most are worth one mark for each fact. Spend about one minute for each mark. The time is our suggestion, not Pearson's: about one minute for each mark. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 5, 36 and 49.)
Listen for how many things you must give. Name two means two answers. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 36.)
Find the exact term you must define or the thing you must name. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 97.)
Think of the full definition from the spec. Check it has every key word, for example interact, or in an area. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 102.)
Write short, exact answers using the biology word, for example sucrose, not sugar. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 37.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Half a definition. An organelle needs the words a specific function. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 6.
Missing the key word. An ecosystem needs the word interact, and a population needs the words in an area. June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 98 and 102.
Mixing up terms. A community is all the species in an area, not one species. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 100.
Vague words, such as sugar instead of sucrose. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 37.
In a gap fill, a wrong word such as hierarchy instead of trophic. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 105.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: What do state, give and name ask for? Answer: Recall of a fact. They mean the same thing. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 5, 36 and 49.)
Ask: What is a population? Answer: All the organisms of one species living in an area. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 5, 36 and 49.)
Ask: What is a community? Answer: All the populations of different species living in an area. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 5, 36 and 49.)
Ask: What is an ecosystem? Answer: A community and its environment, interacting with each other. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 5, 36 and 49.)
Ask: Name two substances carried in the phloem. Answer: Sucrose and amino acids. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 5, 36 and 49.)

Describe means give an account of something. Your statements link together, but you do not need to give reasons. These test knowledge, assessment objective 1, or using data, assessment objective 2. In June 2025 they were worth two to four marks. Spend two to four minutes. The time is our suggestion, not Pearson's: about one minute for each mark. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 78 and 80.)
Listen for what you must describe: a process, a method, or a pattern in data. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 80.)
Mark the command word describe, the topic, and the number of marks. (Source: spec page 45.)
Make one point for each mark. Put the steps in the order they happen. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 8.)
Write each step as a short sentence. For data, say the trend first, then add a detail such as a number or where it levels off. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 44.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Naming two enzymes but not saying what each one does. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 108.
Describing data too briefly. Add a detail, such as a turning point or a number. June 2025 Paper 2 report pages 44 and 45.
Vague statements, such as harmful toxins. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 8.
Fewer points than there are marks. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 8.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: Does describe need a reason? Answer: No. Give an account, in linked steps. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 78 and 80.)
Ask: How many points for a four mark describe? Answer: At least four different points. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 78 and 80.)
Ask: Describe how to measure the area of a leaf. Answer: Draw round it on squared paper and count the squares. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 78 and 80.)

Ask: After the trend, what should a data description add? Answer: A detail, such as a number, a turning point, or where it levels off. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 78 and 80.)
Ask: Which cells make antibodies? Answer: Lymphocytes. Phagocytes engulf pathogens. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 78 and 80.)

Explain means give a point and a reason for it. Your answer must say why or how. These test knowledge and using it, assessment objectives 1 and 2. In June 2025 they were worth two to four marks. Spend three to four minutes. The time is our suggestion, not Pearson's: about one minute for each mark. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 7, 22 and 32.)
Read every word of the question, not just the key words. The context matters. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2 report page 16.)
Mark the word explain, the topic, and any data or diagram you must use. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 7.)
For each point, add because or so. That turns a fact into an explanation. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 23.)
Use exact biology words: oxygen, not air. Respiration releases energy, it does not produce it. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 33.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Saying what to do but not why. In the dark for a day needs the reason: respiration uses up the starch. June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 23 and 25.
Writing air instead of oxygen. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 33.
Saying respiration produces energy. It releases energy. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 16.
Not enough detail. Nitrates are needed to make amino acids for proteins. June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 30 and 31.
Answering a different question, for example writing about the kidney when it asked about the large intestine. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 18.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: What must every explain answer have? Answer: A reason. Use the words because or so. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 7, 22 and 32.)
Ask: How do you remove starch from a leaf? Answer: Keep the plant in the dark for 24 hours. Respiration uses up the starch. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 7, 22 and 32.)

Ask: Why can roots in waterlogged soil not take in minerals? Answer: No oxygen, so less respiration and less energy for active transport. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 7, 22 and 32.)
Ask: What does respiration do with energy? Answer: It releases energy. It does not produce it. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 7, 22 and 32.)
Ask: Why do plants need magnesium? Answer: To make chlorophyll. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 7, 22 and 32.)

Calculate means get a number, and show your working. You may use a calculator. There is no formula sheet, so learn mean, percentage, rate, probability, standard form and significant figures. These test assessment objectives 2 and 3. In June 2025 they were worth two or three marks. Spend two to three minutes. The time is our suggestion, not Pearson's: about one minute for each mark. (Source: spec pages 28, 43 and 45; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 60, 74 and 84.)
Listen for what to work out, and any instruction such as give your answer in standard form. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 84.)
Mark the numbers you need, the units, and words like per day, percentage, or significant figures. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 74.)
Choose the sum. A rate is the change divided by the time. A percentage is the part divided by the total, times one hundred. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 60.)
Write every step of working. Put the answer on the answer line with its unit, in the form asked. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 62.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
No working shown, so no marks for a wrong answer. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 62.
The right number, but not in standard form when asked. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 90.
Mixing up significant figures and decimal places. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 40.
Units not changed, for example centimetres to millimetres. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 70.
Percentage change divided by the wrong number, or not turned into a percentage. June 2025 Paper 2 report pages 82 and 86.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: Why show your working? Answer: You can still get marks if the final answer is wrong. (Source: spec pages 28, 43 and 45; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 60, 74 and 84.)
Ask: How do you find a rate per day? Answer: Divide the change by the number of days. (Source: spec pages 28, 43 and 45; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 60, 74 and 84.)
Ask: How do you find the chance of two things both happening? Answer: Multiply the two probabilities together. (Source: spec pages 28, 43 and 45; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 60, 74 and 84.)
Ask: How do you find a percentage change? Answer: The change, divided by the starting value, times one hundred. (Source: spec pages 28, 43 and 45; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 60, 74 and 84.)

Ask: Is three point five times ten to the six in standard form? Answer: Yes. One number from one to ten, times ten to a power. (Source: spec pages 28, 43 and 45; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 60, 74 and 84.)

Plot means mark points on a grid and draw a line, with a scale and labelled axes. Complete and label mean add to a table, diagram or passage. A genetic diagram shows parents, gametes, offspring genotypes and phenotypes. In June 2025 a graph was worth about five marks, and a genetic diagram four. Spend four to six minutes on a graph. The time is our suggestion, not Pearson's: about one minute for each mark. (Source: spec pages 45 and 46; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 26, 53 and 67.)
Listen for what to show: a graph, labels, a genetic diagram, or missing words. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 67.)
Mark plot, label or complete, and every part asked for, such as gametes or ratio. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 53.)
For a graph, choose a scale that uses most of the grid. Put the thing you changed along the bottom. (Source: spec page 46.)
Plot with a sharp pencil, then join or draw the line. Label everything. Read gap fill sentences in full. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 26.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
One point plotted in the wrong place. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 73.
A diagram shaded but not labelled. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 27.
A genetic diagram with no offspring phenotypes. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 55.
Gap fill words that do not make sense in the whole sentence. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 55.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: What must a graph have? Answer: A sensible scale, labelled axes with units, accurate points, and a line. (Source: spec pages 45 and 46; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 26, 53 and 67.)
Ask: Which variable goes along the bottom? Answer: The independent variable, the one you change. (Source: spec pages 45 and 46; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 26, 53 and 67.)

Ask: What are the four parts of a genetic diagram? Answer: Parent genotypes, gametes, offspring genotypes, and offspring phenotypes. (Source: spec pages 45 and 46; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 26, 53 and 67.)
Ask: What colour shows starch with iodine? Answer: Blue black. No starch stays orange. (Source: spec pages 45 and 46; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 26, 53 and 67.)
Ask: What should you do after filling a gap? Answer: Read the whole sentence again to check it makes sense. (Source: spec pages 45 and 46; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 26, 53 and 67.)

Practical questions ask about variables, safe methods, and how to plan or improve an experiment. The last question in June 2025 asked you to design a whole investigation, for six marks. These test experimental skills, assessment objective 3. Spend about one minute for each mark, and six to seven minutes on a design. The time is our suggestion, not Pearson's: about one minute for each mark. (Source: spec page 28; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 9, 65 and 111.)
Listen for the task: name a variable, give a method, improve it, or design it. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 111.)
Find what is changed, the independent variable, and what is measured, the dependent variable. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 65.)
For a design, cover each part: what you change and its range, what you measure and how, what you keep the same, and repeats. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 115.)
Write steps in order with real amounts and times. Name safe equipment, such as a water bath. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 12.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Giving something that is not a control variable, or giving the independent variable instead. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 11, and Paper 2 report page 50.
Not naming the dependent variable, the thing measured. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 66.
Saying repeat it to make results more accurate. Repeats improve reliability, not accuracy. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 52.
A method that never says what is measured. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 73.
A design that misses the range, how to measure, or how to keep controls the same. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 115.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: What is the independent variable? Answer: The one thing you change on purpose. (Source: spec page 28; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 9, 65 and 111.)
Ask: What is the dependent variable? Answer: The thing you measure. (Source: spec page 28; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 9, 65 and 111.)
Ask: Why use a water bath? Answer: To keep the temperature steady, safely. (Source: spec page 28; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 9, 65 and 111.)
Ask: Do repeats make results more accurate? Answer: No. Repeats make them more reliable. (Source: spec page 28; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 9, 65 and 111.)
Ask: Name four parts of a good design. Answer: What you change and its range, what you measure and how, controls, and repeats. (Source: spec page 28; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 9, 65 and 111.)

Discuss, comment on and evaluate ask you to use the data and your own knowledge, look at more than one side, and come to a judgement. In June 2025 these were worth five marks each. They test assessment objectives 2 and 3. Spend five to six minutes. The time is our suggestion, not Pearson's: about one minute for each mark. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 41 and 93.)
Listen for use the data and your own knowledge. You need both. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 41.)
Mark discuss, comment or evaluate, the topic, and the marks. Five marks needs five points. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 115.)
List what the data shows, then the biology reason for each part. Note a point for and a point against. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 93.)
Quote a number, say when it changes, then give the reason. End with a short judgement. (Source: June 2025 Paper 1 report page 94.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here.
Fewer points than there are marks. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 115.
Quoting numbers without linking them to biology, for example red cell numbers and oxygen transport. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 96.
General statements, such as harm to the environment. June 2025 Paper 1 report page 47.
Looking at one side only, or copying data without working with it. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 60.
Saying it goes up and down without saying when. June 2025 Paper 2 report page 75.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: What two things do discuss questions need? Answer: Information from the data, and your own knowledge. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 41 and 93.)
Ask: How many points for five marks? Answer: At least five different points. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 41 and 93.)
Ask: Is harm to the environment a good point? Answer: No. It is too general. Say exactly what is harmed. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 41 and 93.)
Ask: Give one advantage of biological control. Answer: For example, no need to reapply it, or no build up of poison in food chains. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 41 and 93.)
Ask: What links more lymphocytes to the body? Answer: More antibodies are made, so infection is fought better. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 1 report pages 41 and 93.)

nodeData.note: Edexcel International GCSE Biology, Paper 2, code 4 B I 1 slash 2 B. One hour and 15 minutes, 70 marks, 38.9 percent of the grade. You may use a calculator. There is no formula sheet. Paper 2 tests all the content, including the extra content shown in bold with a letter B in the spec. That is the big difference from Paper 1, which leaves the bold content out. Paper 2 is shorter than Paper 1, which is two hours for 110 marks. It always starts with a reading passage. Each branch is one type of question: read the question, find the key words, plan, write, check. Then five spoken questions. Draft: needs review by a biology teacher. (Source: spec pages 8 and 27; June 2025 Paper 2B report page 3.)

children.note: Paper 2 always starts with a reading passage. The questions after it come from many different topics. In June 2025 the passage was about water pollution, and each part was worth one to four marks. This is new on Paper 2: Paper 1 has no passage. Spend a few minutes reading the passage before you answer. The time is our suggestion, not Pearson's: Paper 2 gives 75 minutes for 70 marks, so about one minute for each mark. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2B report page 3.)
Read the passage slowly first. Then read every word of each question, not just the key words. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2B report page 3.)
Find the exact place or thing the question is about, for example salt in the large intestine, not the kidney. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2B report page 18.)
Do not copy words from the passage. Plan to add your own biology to what the passage says. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2B report page 26.)
Give a clear example. If the question says pollution, name one, such as algae growing in the river. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2B report page 24.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here in the June 2025 Paper 2B report.
Copying a phrase from the passage, such as less nitrate runoff. It gains no marks. June 2025 Paper 2B report page 26.
Writing about the kidney when the question was about the large intestine. June 2025 Paper 2B report page 18.
Saying pollution without an example, such as algal growth. June 2025 Paper 2B report page 24.
Vague answers, such as trees block water. June 2025 Paper 2B report page 27.
Writing an answer in another part of the booklet. Use extra paper instead. June 2025 Paper 2B report page 28.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: How does Paper 2 always begin? Answer: With a reading passage, then questions from many topics. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2B report page 3.)
Ask: What do denitrifying bacteria do? Answer: They turn nitrates into nitrogen gas. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2B report page 3.)

Ask: How can fertiliser in a river kill fish? Answer: Algae grow and block light. Plants die and bacteria decompose them. The bacteria use up the oxygen, so fish cannot respire. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2B report page 3.)
Ask: How do trees help stop flooding? Answer: Their roots take up water, they lose water by transpiration, and they hold the soil together. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2B report page 3.)
Ask: Should you copy words from the passage? Answer: No. Use your own biology to add detail. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2B report page 3.)

State, give and name all mean recall a fact. Most are worth one mark for each fact. In June 2025 Paper 2 asked for a definition of homeostasis for one mark, the job of FSH for one mark, and two differences between DNA and RNA for two marks. Paper 2 can ask about the bold B content too, such as DNA, RNA and the menstrual hormones. Spend about one minute for each mark. The time is our suggestion, not Pearson's: Paper 2 gives 75 minutes for 70 marks, so about one minute for each mark. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 2B report page 4, 12 and 93.)
Listen for how many things you must give. Two differences means two separate points. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2B report page 95.)
Find the exact term you must define, such as homeostasis. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2B report page 4.)
Recall the full meaning from the spec. Learn every word in the spec, including the bold B words. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2B report page 4.)
Write a short, exact answer. Say exactly what the hormone does, for example FSH makes eggs mature. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2B report page 12.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here in the June 2025 Paper 2B report.
Defining homeostasis as temperature control only. It means keeping all internal conditions steady. June 2025 Paper 2B report page 5.
Mixing up the jobs of FSH and LH. June 2025 Paper 2B report page 12.
Saying FSH acts on the ovaries, but not that it makes eggs mature. June 2025 Paper 2B report page 13.
Giving the same difference twice. Thymine in DNA and uracil in RNA count as one point. June 2025 Paper 2B report page 95.
Swapping them round, saying RNA has thymine and DNA has uracil. June 2025 Paper 2B report page 93.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: What is homeostasis? Answer: Keeping the conditions inside the body steady. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 2B report page 4, 12 and 93.)
Ask: What does FSH do? Answer: It makes eggs mature in the ovary. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 2B report page 4, 12 and 93.)
Ask: What does LH do? Answer: It makes the ovary release an egg. This is ovulation. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 2B report page 4, 12 and 93.)

Ask: Give two differences between DNA and RNA. Answer: DNA has two strands in a double helix, RNA has one strand. DNA has thymine, RNA has uracil. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 2B report page 4, 12 and 93.)
Ask: What does ADH do? Answer: It makes the kidney take back more water into the blood. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 2B report page 4, 12 and 93.)

Describe means give an account. Your points link together, but you do not need reasons. In June 2025 Paper 2 asked you to describe data from a table for two marks, and a four mark answer asked how farming pollutes rivers. Spend two to four minutes. The time is our suggestion, not Pearson's: Paper 2 gives 75 minutes for 70 marks, so about one minute for each mark. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 2B report page 8 and 44.)
Listen for what you must describe: a pattern in data, or a process. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2B report page 44.)
Mark the word describe, the marks, and the units in the table. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2B report page 44.)
Make one point for each mark. Put the events in the order they happen, like a story. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2B report page 9.)
Say the trend first. Then add a detail: a number, the biggest change, or where it levels off. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2B report page 44.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here in the June 2025 Paper 2B report.
Giving only the trend, with no turning point or levelling off. June 2025 Paper 2B report page 45.
Not working with the data. Working out a change, such as 6.2 millimetres, can earn the second mark. June 2025 Paper 2B report page 46.
Vague statements, such as harmful toxins. June 2025 Paper 2B report page 8.
Fewer points than there are marks. June 2025 Paper 2B report page 8.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.
Ask: Does describe need a reason? Answer: No. Give an account, in linked steps. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 2B report page 8 and 44.)
Ask: How many points for a two mark data question? Answer: Two. The trend, then a detail. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 2B report page 8 and 44.)
Ask: What happens to the pupil as light gets brighter? Answer: It gets narrower, then levels off. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 2B report page 8 and 44.)
Ask: Name three details you can add after a trend. Answer: A number, the biggest change, or where it levels off. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 2B report page 8 and 44.)

Ask: Put eutrophication in order. Answer: Fertiliser runs off, algae grow, light is blocked, plants die, bacteria decompose them and use up oxygen. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 2B report page 8 and 44.)

Explain means give a point and a reason. Most Paper 2 marks in June 2025 came from explain questions, worth two to four marks each. Many were about bold B content only on Paper 2: the kidney tubule, the iris, and protein synthesis. Spend three to four minutes. The time is our suggestion, not Pearson's: Paper 2 gives 75 minutes for 70 marks, so about one minute for each mark. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 2B report page 16, 36 and 96.)
Read every word of the question. When you are nervous, it is easy to spot one key word and miss the context. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2B report page 16.)
Mark the exact part of the body, such as the proximal convoluted tubule, and the process, such as active transport. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2B report page 36.)
Use the exact words from the spec, such as transcription, translation, codon and anticodon. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2B report page 96.)
Link each point with because or so. Then read your answer back, to check you wrote pH and not temperature. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2B report page 87.)
Read your answer again and check it for each of these. The examiners saw students lose marks here in the June 2025 Paper 2B report.
Confusing resistance with immunity. Bacteria do not make antibodies. June 2025 Paper 2B report page 20.
Confusing the ciliary muscles of the lens with the muscles of the iris. June 2025 Paper 2B report page 47.
Not naming the proximal convoluted tubule, or active transport. June 2025 Paper 2B report page 36.
Writing optimum temperature when the question was about pH. June 2025 Paper 2B report page 87.
Mixing up transcription and translation. June 2025 Paper 2B report page 96.
Say each question out loud, answer it out loud, then open the bubble to check. Do this before you start and again at the end. No score is kept, and you can try again as often as you like.

Ask: How do bacteria become resistant to antibiotics? Answer: A mutation gives resistance. Those bacteria survive, reproduce, and pass on the allele. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 2B report page 16, 36 and 96.)

Ask: Why does the pupil narrow in bright light? Answer: Circular muscles contract and radial muscles relax, so less light reaches the retina. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 2B report page 16, 36 and 96.)

Ask: Why is there glucose in diabetic urine? Answer: The proximal convoluted tubule cannot take back all the glucose by active transport. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 2B report page 16, 36 and 96.)

Ask: What happens to an enzyme far from its best pH? Answer: It denatures. The active site changes shape, so the substrate cannot fit. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 2B report page 16, 36 and 96.)

Ask: What are transcription and translation? Answer: Transcription copies DNA into messenger RNA. Translation builds the protein at the ribosome, with transfer RNA bringing amino acids. (Source: spec page 45; June 2025 Paper 2B report page 16, 36 and 96.)

Calculate means get a number and show your working. You may use a calculator, and there is no formula sheet. In June 2025 Paper 2 had four calculations: two means, a rate, and a percentage increase, each worth two marks. Spend about two minutes on each. The time is our suggestion, not Pearson's: Paper 2 gives 75 minutes for 70 marks, so about one minute for each mark. (Source: spec page 43; June 2025 Paper 2B report page 6, 40, 68 and 80.)
Listen for instructions such as give your answer to two significant figures. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2B report page 40.)
Mark the units. If the data is in centimetres and the answer is in millimetres, convert first. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2B report page 68.)

Ask: On a lung volume graph, what does a rising line show? Answer: Breathing in. The lungs are getting bigger. (Source: spec page 46; June 2025 Paper 2B report page 31, 55 and 80.)

Practical questions ask about variables, accuracy, and methods. In June 2025 Paper 2 asked for a control variable for one mark, how to make results accurate for two marks, and a method using a potometer, a bold B practical, where good answers gained four marks. Paper 2 can use the bold B practicals, such as transpiration and enzymes with pH. Spend about one minute for each mark. The time is our suggestion, not Pearson's: Paper 2 gives 75 minutes for 70 marks, so about one minute for each mark. (Source: spec pages 17 and 28; June 2025 Paper 2B report page 50, 52 and 71.)
Listen for the task: name a variable, make it more accurate, or describe a method. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2B report page 52.)
Is the question about accuracy or reliability? Repeats make results reliable. They do not make them accurate. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2B report page 90.)

Ask: What does a potometer measure? Answer: How fast a shoot takes up water, from how far a bubble moves. (Source: spec pages 17 and 28; June 2025 Paper 2B report page 50, 52 and 71.)
Ask: Why cut the shoot under water? Answer: To stop air getting into the xylem. (Source: spec pages 17 and 28; June 2025 Paper 2B report page 50, 52 and 71.)

Ask: How can you judge a colour change more accurately? Answer: Use a colour chart or a colorimeter, and check more often. (Source: spec pages 17 and 28; June 2025 Paper 2B report page 50, 52 and 71.)
Ask: What do repeats improve? Answer: Reliability, not accuracy. (Source: spec pages 17 and 28; June 2025 Paper 2B report page 50, 52 and 71.)

Ask: Name two controls for a wind speed and transpiration test. Answer: Any two of temperature, humidity, light intensity, or the same plant. (Source: spec pages 17 and 28; June 2025 Paper 2B report page 50, 52 and 71.)

Spend five to six minutes on each. The time is our suggestion, not Pearson's: Paper 2 gives 75 minutes for 70 marks, so about one minute for each mark. Ask: Why might a cloned pet behave differently? Answer: The environment affects behaviour, not just the genes. (Source: June 2025 Paper 2B report page 3, 60 and 75.)
